questions.question: What is a Virtual Machine (VM)?

options.text: A container running on Docker
A software-based computer that runs on a physical server with its own OS
A Docker image stored in a registry
A Kubernetes pod

explanation.correct: A VM is a software-based computer created by a hypervisor on a physical server. Each VM has its own complete operating system and pre-allocated resources.
explanation.why: A is a container, not a VM. C is a Docker image. D is a Kubernetes concept.

questions.question: What is the primary role of a hypervisor?

options.text: To compile source code into executable format
To manage Docker containers at scale
To create and manage virtual machines by partitioning physical hardware
To store Docker images remotely

explanation.correct: A hypervisor sits between physical hardware and VMs, partitioning resources like CPU, RAM, and disk to create isolated virtual machines.
explanation.why: A describes a compiler. B describes Kubernetes. D describes a Docker registry.

questions.question: What does the git commit command do?

options.text: Uploads code to GitHub
Creates a versioned snapshot of staged files in the local repository
Merges a feature branch into main
Downloads the latest code from a remote repository

explanation.correct: git commit creates a permanent snapshot (version) of all staged files in the local .git repository. It does not upload anything to GitHub.
explanation.why: A is git push. C is done via a Pull Request merge. D is git pull.

questions.question: What is a Dockerfile?

options.text: A running container instance
A remote image storage location
A plain text file with step-by-step instructions to build a Docker image
A Kubernetes configuration file

explanation.correct: A Dockerfile is a plain text blueprint containing instructions (FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD) that Docker reads to build a container image.
explanation.why: A is a container, not a Dockerfile. B is a Docker registry. D is typically a YAML manifest file.

questions.question: Which Docker command builds an image from a Dockerfile?

options.text: docker run
docker pull
docker build
docker push

explanation.correct: docker build reads the Dockerfile and creates a Docker image. The -t flag names and tags the image.
explanation.why: docker run creates a container from an image. docker pull downloads an image. docker push uploads an image to a registry.

questions.question: What is a Docker container?

options.text: A read-only template that stores application files
A running instance of a Docker image — a live, isolated process
A file that lists Docker build instructions
A remote storage location for images

explanation.correct: A Docker container is what you get when you run a Docker image. It is a live, isolated process executing the application with its own filesystem and network.
explanation.why: A describes a Docker image. C describes a Dockerfile. D describes a Docker registry.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the FROM instruction in a Dockerfile?

options.text: To expose a network port
To copy files into the container
To specify the base image the container starts from
To run a command inside the container at runtime

explanation.correct: FROM specifies the base image — the starting point for the container. Every container must start from some base (e.g., python:3.11, nginx, ubuntu).
explanation.why: EXPOSE handles ports. COPY copies files. CMD specifies the runtime command.

questions.question: What does CI stand for in CI/CD?

options.text: Container Integration
Continuous Integration
Cloud Infrastructure
Code Inspection

explanation.correct: CI stands for Continuous Integration — the practice of automatically building and testing code every time a developer pushes a change.
explanation.why: Container Integration and Code Inspection are not standard terms. Cloud Infrastructure is unrelated to CI/CD.

questions.question: Which tool is most commonly used for static code analysis in CI pipelines?

options.text: JUnit
Maven
SonarQube
Jenkins

explanation.correct: SonarQube is the most popular static code analysis tool. It examines code without running it to find bugs, code smells, and security vulnerabilities.
explanation.why: JUnit is for unit testing. Maven is a build tool. Jenkins is a CI orchestration tool.

questions.question: What is a Pull Request (PR) in Git?

options.text: A command to download code from GitHub
A request to merge a feature branch into the main branch, reviewed by a team lead
A Docker image pushed to a registry
A CI pipeline trigger event

explanation.correct: A Pull Request is a formal request in GitHub/GitLab to merge your feature branch into the main branch. A code reviewer checks the changes before approving.
explanation.why: git pull downloads code. Docker push uploads images. A CI trigger is a webhook event.

questions.question: Which key difference exists between a Virtual Machine and a Container regarding the operating system?

options.text: VMs share the host OS kernel; containers run a full OS each
Containers share the host OS kernel; VMs each run a full OS
Both share the host OS kernel
Both run full independent operating systems

explanation.correct: This is the fundamental architectural difference. Containers share the host OS kernel (making them lightweight), while each VM runs its own full Guest OS (making them heavier).
explanation.why: VMs do not share the host kernel — they are fully isolated at the hardware level.

questions.question: What is Docker Hub?

options.text: A CI/CD pipeline tool
A public Docker image registry where images can be stored and pulled
A container orchestration platform
A Kubernetes management dashboard

explanation.correct: Docker Hub is the most popular public Docker registry. Developers push images to it and pull base images like nginx, python, or ubuntu from it.
explanation.why: Jenkins is a CI/CD tool. Kubernetes is the orchestration platform. Kubernetes Dashboard exists but is separate.

questions.question: When exactly does the CI pipeline trigger automatically?

options.text: Only when code is pushed directly to main
Only when a Pull Request is merged
When code is pushed to main OR when a Pull Request is created or updated
Only when the team lead manually starts it

explanation.correct: The CI pipeline triggers on two events: when code is pushed to main (or any branch configured), and when a PR is created or updated. This ensures code is always validated before and after merge.
explanation.why: Limiting triggers to only one event would miss validation opportunities and defeat the purpose of continuous integration.

questions.question: What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?

options.text: They are identical — the terms are interchangeable
Continuous Delivery requires manual approval before production; Continuous Deployment deploys automatically
Continuous Deployment requires manual approval; Continuous Delivery is fully automatic
Continuous Delivery is only for containers; Continuous Deployment is for VMs

explanation.correct: Continuous Delivery means code is always ready to deploy but a human approves the production push. Continuous Deployment goes one step further — production is updated automatically after all tests pass.
explanation.why: These are distinct practices. Most organizations use Continuous Delivery, keeping a manual gate for production deployments.

questions.question: What is the purpose of git add before git commit?

options.text: It creates a new branch
It uploads files to GitHub
It moves modified files into the staging area, ready to be committed
It merges changes into the main branch

explanation.correct: git add moves files from the working directory into the staging area (buffer zone). Only staged files are included in the next git commit snapshot.
explanation.why: Branch creation uses git checkout -b. Uploading uses git push. Merging uses a Pull Request or git merge.

questions.question: In Docker, what does the -p 8080:80 flag mean in docker run -p 8080:80 my-app?

options.text: Expose port 8080 inside the container and 80 on the host
Map port 8080 on the host machine to port 80 inside the container
Run the container on 8080 threads with 80MB RAM
Connect to 8080 containers simultaneously using 80 cores

explanation.correct: The format is host:container. -p 8080:80 means traffic arriving at port 8080 on the host is forwarded to port 80 inside the container.
explanation.why: The host port is always listed first. Containers expose their own internal port (80 for nginx), and you map it to a host port of your choice.

questions.question: What is the role of Terraform in a CI/CD pipeline?

options.text: Running unit tests on application code
Building Docker images from Dockerfiles
Provisioning infrastructure such as EC2 instances, VPCs, and databases as code
Orchestrating containers across multiple nodes

explanation.correct: Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code tool that provisions cloud infrastructure — creating EC2 instances, VPCs, security groups, databases — in an automated, repeatable way.
explanation.why: Unit tests use JUnit/PyTest. Docker build creates images. Kubernetes orchestrates containers.

questions.question: What is code coverage in the context of a CI pipeline?

options.text: The percentage of code reviewed by the team lead before merging
A measure of how much of the codebase is exercised by automated tests
The number of lines of code written per sprint
The SonarQube score for code quality

explanation.correct: Code coverage measures what percentage of your source code is actually executed by your unit tests. High coverage means more of the code is validated automatically.
explanation.why: Code review is manual. Lines of code is a productivity metric. SonarQube gives a quality score, not a coverage percentage specifically.

questions.question: Which AWS service is the native equivalent of GitHub for storing Git repositories?

options.text: AWS CodeBuild
AWS CodeDeploy
AWS CodeCommit
Amazon ECR

explanation.correct: AWS CodeCommit is AWS's managed Git repository service — the AWS equivalent of GitHub or GitLab. It stores source code with full Git support.
explanation.why: CodeBuild is a CI build service. CodeDeploy automates deployments. ECR stores Docker images, not source code.

questions.question: What makes containers more portable than virtual machines?

options.text: Containers include a full OS, so they are self-contained
Containers package the application with its dependencies into a single image that runs identically anywhere Docker is installed
Containers use more RAM, giving them better performance
Containers are always stored in AWS, making them globally accessible

explanation.correct: A Docker image bundles the application code, runtime, and libraries together. Since it doesn't depend on the host OS beyond the kernel, it runs identically on any machine with Docker — laptop, EC2, or Kubernetes.
explanation.why: Containers do NOT include a full OS. More RAM usage is a disadvantage of VMs, not containers. Images are stored in registries, not inherently in AWS.

questions.question: A developer hardcodes an AWS access key directly in a Python script and pushes it to GitHub. Which CI pipeline stage would flag this as a critical security issue?

options.text: Compile / Build stage
Unit Testing stage
Static Code Analysis (SonarQube)
Code Coverage stage

explanation.correct: Static code analysis tools like SonarQube scan code without running it and specifically look for hardcoded credentials and security vulnerabilities. This is a critical security finding it would immediately flag.
explanation.why: Compile/Build only checks syntax and creates the executable. Unit tests verify logic. Code coverage measures test completeness.

questions.question: What is the role of Kubernetes in relation to Docker?

options.text: Kubernetes replaces Docker completely and does not use Docker images
Kubernetes orchestrates and manages containers (often Docker containers) at scale across multiple nodes
Kubernetes is used to build Docker images in CI pipelines
Kubernetes is a Docker registry for storing images

explanation.correct: Docker creates and runs individual containers. Kubernetes orchestrates those containers at scale — managing scheduling, scaling, self-healing, and load balancing across a cluster of nodes.
explanation.why: Kubernetes uses container images (often Docker-compatible). It does not replace Docker's image format. It doesn't build images or store them.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of Docker image layering?

options.text: Each layer encrypts the application code for security
Docker can cache unchanged layers and only rebuild the layers that have changed, making builds faster
Layers allow multiple applications to share the same container
Layers eliminate the need for a Dockerfile

explanation.correct: Docker builds images in layers — one per Dockerfile instruction. Each layer is cached. If only your application code changes (COPY instruction), Docker only rebuilds that layer and above, skipping the base OS and library layers. This dramatically speeds up CI/CD builds.
explanation.why: Layers are not encrypted. Containers run one application process by design. Dockerfiles are still required.

questions.question: An EC2 instance running 15 Docker containers crashes. What is the impact compared to 15 separate EC2 instances each running one application?

options.text: The impact is the same — all 15 services go down in both scenarios
With containers on one EC2, all 15 services go down; with separate EC2s, only the one that crashed is affected
With containers, only the crashed container is affected; with separate EC2s, all go down
Containers automatically restart on a different EC2 without any configuration

explanation.correct: This is a single point of failure problem. Running all containers on one EC2 means if that EC2 fails, all services fail. Separate EC2 instances provide VM-level isolation so only the failed instance affects its single service.
explanation.why: This is why Kubernetes spreads containers across multiple nodes — to avoid single points of failure. Auto-restart across nodes requires Kubernetes or ECS, not Docker alone.

questions.question: In a microservices architecture, the payment service has a memory leak and crashes. What happens to the product catalogue service running in its own container?

options.text: The product catalogue service also crashes because they share the same container runtime
The product catalogue service continues running normally because it is isolated in a separate container
The product catalogue service automatically takes over payment processing
Kubernetes immediately deletes the product catalogue container as a precaution

explanation.correct: Container isolation ensures that a failure in one container does not propagate to other containers. The product catalogue has its own process space, memory, and filesystem — unaffected by the payment service crash.
explanation.why: This is one of the core benefits of containerized microservices over monolithic applications where one failing component can bring down the entire application.

questions.question: Which AWS service provides a fully managed Docker image registry equivalent to Docker Hub?

options.text: Amazon ECS
Amazon EKS
Amazon ECR
AWS CodeBuild

explanation.correct: Amazon ECR (Elastic Container Registry) is AWS's managed Docker image registry. It integrates natively with ECS and EKS for seamless image pulling during deployments.
explanation.why: ECS runs containers. EKS manages Kubernetes clusters. CodeBuild is a CI build service.

questions.question: A team uses Ansible and Terraform in their CD pipeline. Which tool provisions the EC2 servers and which tool deploys the application?

options.text: Ansible provisions EC2; Terraform deploys applications
Terraform provisions EC2; Ansible deploys and configures the application on the server
Both Terraform and Ansible provision EC2 instances simultaneously
Terraform deploys containers; Ansible creates Docker images

explanation.correct: Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code tool for provisioning cloud infrastructure — creating EC2, VPCs, security groups. Ansible is a software configuration management tool for deploying and configuring applications on those servers.
explanation.why: These tools have complementary, not overlapping, roles in the pipeline. Terraform creates the environment; Ansible configures and deploys software into it.

questions.question: A Docker build fails at the RUN npm install step. The error is 'package not found'. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The Dockerfile does not have a FROM instruction
The package.json file was not copied into the container before running npm install
Docker Hub is unavailable
The container is missing a CMD instruction

explanation.correct: npm install reads package.json to know which packages to install. If COPY is missing or placed after RUN, package.json doesn't exist in the container when npm install runs. The correct order is: COPY package.json → RUN npm install → COPY source code.
explanation.why: FROM is required and the build wouldn't start without it. Docker Hub unavailability would show a network error. CMD is for runtime, not build time.

questions.question: What is the git fork operation and when would you use it?

options.text: Fork creates a local copy of a branch on your laptop
Fork creates your own copy of someone else's repository in your GitHub account, used for contributing to open source projects
Fork splits the main branch into two parallel branches
Fork deletes all feature branches after a merge

explanation.correct: git fork (done via the GitHub UI, not a git command) creates a complete copy of another user's repository in your own GitHub account. You can then modify it freely and raise a Pull Request back to the original. It is the standard workflow for open source contributions.
explanation.why: git clone creates a local copy. Branching creates parallel development lines. There is no auto-delete on fork.

questions.question: Why is the Docker Daemon (dockerd) separate from the Docker Client (CLI)?

options.text: The daemon runs in the cloud while the client runs locally
The separation allows remote management — the CLI can talk to a daemon running on a different machine, and keeps the interface simple while the engine handles complexity
The client builds images and the daemon only stores them
They cannot run on the same machine simultaneously

explanation.correct: The client-server architecture of Docker separates the interface (CLI) from the engine (daemon). This allows remote Docker management — your local docker command can control a daemon on a remote server. It also makes the system extensible and the client lightweight.
explanation.why: Both run locally by default but can be remote. The daemon does all work including builds. They absolutely can and do run on the same machine.
